Comparisons

Whey concentrate vs isolate vs plant protein: price, ingredients and suitability compared

Compare like-for-like servings, dietary requirements and value.

By Nutrition.Fitness · 15 September 2026 · 4 min read

The short answer

Choose protein powder by dietary suitability, the actual label and cost for the amount of protein you receive. Whey concentrate and isolate come from milk; isolate is more filtered but is not automatically lactose-free. Plant products vary and still require allergen checks. None is compulsory. Food may already meet your needs, and a higher price does not by itself justify an upgrade.

The best-value powder is one that fits your dietary needs, supplies a useful amount of protein and is something you are willing to use. There is no universal winner between whey concentrate, whey isolate and plant protein. Start with suitability, then compare the figures.

Nutrition.Fitness's offer includes supplements, so we have a commercial interest in this subject. They are optional purchases, separate from NUFI. This is a label-and-price comparison, not hands-on testing, and it cannot tell you which flavour you will enjoy.

What the names tell you

TypeWhat to checkWhen it may suit
Whey concentrateMilk-based ingredients, protein content and other ingredients in the chosen flavourYou use dairy and want a convenient protein option at a suitable price
Whey isolateAdditional filtration, actual protein content and lactose informationYou have a specific reason to prefer its composition and the extra cost is justified
Plant proteinThe protein source or blend, label values and all allergen warningsYou want to avoid animal ingredients or prefer a particular plant-based product

The selected 900g vanilla Impact Whey concentrate was marked out of stock when checked. Its displayed price is a comparison snapshot, not a currently available purchase.

Myprotein's isolate product information describes extra filtration and states that the product is not completely lactose-free. An isolate label is therefore not a reason to assume it will suit every person with digestive symptoms.

A real label snapshot, with its limits

These UK product-page figures were checked on 15 September 2026. They compare three examples from one manufacturer, not the whole market. Prices shown are the displayed product prices before delivery or anything used to mix the powder. Promotions, stock and selected flavours can change. Check the packet and final basket before ordering.

Displayed examplePack and priceProtein per 100gCalculated cost per 25g protein
Impact Whey Protein, vanilla900g, £31.9972g£1.23
Impact Whey Isolate, vanilla900g, £39.9982g£1.35
Impact Vegan Protein, strawberry1kg, £20.0073g£0.68

These calculations use the nutritional tables displayed with those product examples, rather than a headline “up to” protein claim. The plant page contained both an unflavoured marketing footnote and a strawberry product description; the table here uses its displayed nutritional panel. Verify the exact purchased variant if values differ.

The comparison shows why an assumed ranking can be misleading. In this snapshot, the plant example has the lowest calculated protein cost. That does not establish that all plant powders are cheapest, or that it is the best product for you.

How to make the same calculation yourself

Multiply the pack weight by its protein proportion to estimate the protein in the pack. Divide the price by that quantity, then multiply by 25. Using the concentrate example: 900g × 0.72 gives 648g protein; £31.99 ÷ 648 × 25 gives approximately £1.23.

The 25g quantity is a comparison unit, not a personalised serving recommendation. Comparing price per scoop can mislead because scoop sizes and protein concentrations differ. Add delivery when calculating the cost of the order you would actually place.

Milk allergy and lactose intolerance are different

The NHS distinguishes lactose intolerance from food allergy. Whey remains milk protein, including whey isolate. Someone with a milk allergy should not treat reduced lactose as making whey suitable.

The plant example uses pea and fava bean protein and states that its facility also handles milk. A vegan description is not an allergy-safety guarantee. Check the full ingredients and precautionary warnings, and follow your clinician's advice where allergy is involved. Repeated digestive symptoms deserve assessment rather than repeated guesses at a different powder.

When paying more may be unnecessary

If you tolerate your current choice, like using it and it meets a practical need, ask what a premium option would improve. A higher protein percentage can matter to a particular comparison, but it does not make a powder essential or turn it into a full meal.

Also compare with ordinary food. If meals already provide what you need, buying powder adds an expense rather than solving a gap. If convenience is the reason, compare the powder with food options you would actually eat, including their preparation and storage.

Before buying a large pack or subscription, check whether a smaller size or sample is available and what it costs. We have not tested these products' taste or mixability. Your next decision is whether you need a powder at all, then which suitable label and delivered price make sense. Browse food-based recipe ideas alongside any supplement comparison.
